On its built-in voices, it comes within half a point of character error rate of a 2.3B-parameter model at under a quarter of the size, and a 7.6M-parameter single-voice model trained with the same recipe matches the most intelligible systems we measured, which suggests that training data matters more for intelligibility than model size. We also report practical findings on voice cloning: conditioning on the reference audio alone, rather than continuing it, cuts skipped words from 21.9% to 1.7%; 20-30 seconds of reference audio works best; and a low-rank adapter trained in about two minutes raises speaker similarity well above instant cloning. Finally, we describe inference-engine changes that bring first audio down to 32 ms for a single stream. We release our evaluation harness and three Turkish speech and text datasets.

abstract: Generative recommendation, has been attracted a surge of attentions in industrial and academic research community, towards to build more smart system to build next-generation recommender. Under the significant developing wave of large language model, our team have been developed Semantic ID based OneRec/OneRec-V2. These models have been widely deployed in production and demonstrate the scaling potential of the autoregressive next-item prediction paradigm for industrial recommender systems. Building on the success of OneRec, we further explored a series of models, including OneRec-Think, OpenOneRec, and OneReason, that connect item Semantic IDs with natural language in a unified representation space and seek to unlock the potential of natural-language chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning for recommendation. However, our preliminary works found that introducing reasoning CoT does not always improve the recommendation performance. To address this issue, OneReason strengthens the semantic alignment between items and language, introduces structured template-based supervision for interest reasoning, and applies advanced reinforcement learning techniques to make reasoning more beneficial to recommendation. As a frontier topic to building recommendation foundation models, we believe this topic has significant research value and hope to encourage more researchers to explore it together. To this end, together with the SIGIR 2026 community, we organized the KUAISHOU Explorer LLM-Rec Challenge 2026: Reasoning Generative Recommendation.

abstract: Question answering over spreadsheet collections requires finding the correct workbook and computing over complete tables. We introduce Find-then-Compute (FiCo), which retrieves document summaries, disambiguates similar workbooks, and executes constrained Structured Query Language (SQL) over the selected full table. On DataBench (80 datasets, 1,810 questions), FiCo reaches 76.2% accuracy: 9.9 points above a strong TableRAG-style baseline on the same frozen workbook choices (66.3%) under the tracks' prespecified evaluators, and 63.4 points above prefix RAG (12.8%). On 508 MiMoTable questions, FiCo reaches 79.7%, versus 22.2% for prefix RAG. Giving the strong baseline the gold workbook raises it from 66.3% to 76.3%, exposing a 10.0-point source-selection cost under fixed compute. Despite 95.1% document recall and 98.5% executable SQL, only 81.3% of questions execute on the gold workbook. FiCo's advantage comes from integrating semantic source selection with exact, schema-grounded computation.

abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models integrate visual perception, language understanding, and action generation to control robots. Testing these systems produces trajectories and task outcomes, but existing approaches provide limited guidance on using these recorded trajectories to assess subsequent executions or inform policy repair. We conjecture that, for a given policy and task, traversing certain workspace regions is associated with a higher likelihood of failure. To investigate this conjecture, we propose VoxelSBFL, a black-box adaptation of Spectrum-Based Fault Localization (SBFL) in which workspace voxels replace program elements as units of analysis. Recorded tool-center-point (TCP) trajectories provide binary voxel coverage, which is combined with execution outcomes to construct suspiciousness maps using established SBFL formulas. These maps identify failure-associated regions and score unseen trajectories without requiring internal model access. We evaluate 34 spectrum-based techniques across four VLA models using 96,000 Pick-Up trajectories in simulation and compare the leading techniques against eight action- and trajectory-based metrics. VoxelSBFL obtains an overall macro ROC-AUC of 0.704, significantly outperforming state-of-the art baselines. Sensitivity analyses show that performance varies with spatial granularity and training-set size. These findings support spatial spectra for VLA execution assessment and motivate future research on runtime monitoring, self-healing and targeted policy improvement.

abstract: Virtual tissue models link observations to mechanistic hypotheses, but building them demands expertise in biology, mathematics and programming. Here, large language model (LLM) agents paired with the simulator Morpheus (Morpheus.AI) autonomously built such models from fifteen benchmark studies, five without a published model. With a frontier LLM, agents that ran their simulations met 83-86% of study-specific criteria in under two hours and for under US\$4 per model. Such agents could make in silico modeling routine.

abstract: We study degenerate preconditioned proximal point algorithms (PPPA) for finding zeros of nonmonotone set-valued operators in Hilbert spaces under solution-relative $(U,V)$-semimonotonicity, with possibly indefinite $U$ and $V$. With a closed-range preconditioner $P$, the reduced PPPA dynamics admit a forward representation through the complementary resolvent of a parallel composition, without requiring monotonicity or admissibility. Relative semimonotonicity of the range-restricted operator transfers to the reduced forward map, allowing our forward theory for possibly set-valued mappings to yield Fejér estimates and residual rates. Under suitable conditions, including demiclosedness of the reduced map at zero, the projected PPPA iterates and shadows converge weakly to a common projected zero. Without demiclosedness, a counterexample shows that the projected sequences may converge to a point outside the projected zero set, even when the original operator is continuous. Bounded recovery condition yields weak convergence of the full (non-projected) shadows. The monotonicity modulus $U$ yields additional results: under suitable conditions, $U\succeqτP$ with $τ>0$ gives strong and linear convergence of the projected PPPA sequences, while $U\succeq-σP$ with $0\leσ<1/2$ still permits local linear rates under metric subregularity. These strong convergence and linear rate guarantees extend to the full shadows when a Lipschitz recovery estimate holds, such as when $U$ is strongly monotone on $\ker P$. For Chambolle--Pock and Douglas--Rachford splitting, we establish Lipschitz recovery even when $U=0$ by exploiting the primal--dual structure. Under suitable parameter conditions, full-shadow convergence guarantees, including $R$-linear rates, extend to the original PPPA iterates.

abstract: Interactive video world models turn user commands into the exploration of a generated scene, which requires the scene to keep its 3D structure as the camera moves and each action to keep a stable effect. Existing benchmarks mostly evaluate these properties against references fitted to the video under test, either a scene reconstructed from its own frames or a camera trajectory aligned to the command path with a free scale. Such references can absorb gradual scene deformation and changes in pace and route length, so these errors can pass undetected. We therefore introduce StrideWorld, a benchmark whose references are fixed before the motion they judge. It evaluates scene rigidity against the ground-truth geometry of the start view, and action consistency against the stride of each action, the camera motion of one command. The stride is measured on the model's first steps and then used to test the steps that follow, so each model is judged only against its own steps. Its measurements are validated on rendered videos with known camera motion, and its scores agree with human judgments. Across \nvideos{} videos generated by \nmodels{} open models from $140$ start views, all models but one deform their scenes as the camera moves, with offsets up to $7.3$ times those of a rigid rendering along the same camera path. Most models keep a steady pace when a single action is held. Along composed routes, several models often stall, and most completed routes end away from the positions predicted by each model's own strides. Only the two models that scale commands by the estimated scene depth bring most routes close to these positions. Fine-tuning two models on a few rendered clips removes most of their mid-route stalls. Code, data, and a leaderboard are publicly available at https://github.com/chuangwang123/strideworld.

abstract: Modern gradient boosting algorithms are based on Newton's method, which excels empirically but lacks global convergence guarantees. While recent work on Gradient-Regularized Newton (GRN) boosting achieved a global $\mathcal{O}(1/γ^{12}k^2)$ rate, its analysis was not able to exploit the natural Hessian geometry and suffers from a heavy $γ^{12}$ dependence on a worst-case `weak gradient edge' $γ$. In this paper, we tackle these theoretical drawbacks by generalizing the Affine-Invariant Cubic Newton (AICN) scheme to convex optimization with weak learners. Our analysis is based on average cosine values $\overlineΘ_k$ along the optimization path and directional improvements $δ_k$ in the Hessian-induced norm. We show that the weak-AICN update reduces to a damped weak-Newton step with an explicit stepsize determined by $δ_k$. Under semi-strong self-concordance, we establish a global $\mathcal{O}(1/\overlineΘ_k^4 k^2)$ rate, significantly improving upon the weak-GRN bound. We further prove a local linear rate, global linear convergence for Hessian-dominated losses, cosine angle lower bounds, and present weak-AdaAICN, which adaptively tunes the cubic regularization. Finally, we demonstrate the broader applicability of this framework beyond gradient boosting by showing that Newton coordinate descent emerges naturally as a special case of optimization with weak learners.

abstract: A backdoored language model behaves normally until a trigger phrase appears in its input. Every published method for recovering such a trigger runs the model. We show the trigger is legible in the weights alone: a static statistic reads a fine-tuned checkpoint with no forward pass of the suspect, no data, no labelled population of poisoned models and no prior knowledge that a backdoor exists, and names one of the tokens of the trigger phrase as the single highest-ranked candidate in the vocabulary.

abstract: Recent image generation models produce photo-realistic results with rich details, but transferring their powerful priors to video restoration remains difficult due to temporal inconsistency from stochastic detail synthesis. Existing video restoration methods improve temporal coherence but often sacrifice visual fidelity, leaving a gap between image-level quality and video-level stability. We propose a generative video restoration method that bridges this gap by enabling temporally consistent detail synthesis from image generation priors. Our method combines noise energy rebalancing to suppress structure-disturbing low-frequency stochasticity, motion-aligned noise warping to propagate details along object motion, a self-supervised denoising encoder to mitigate encoder-induced temporal uncertainty, and decoupled temporal attention to model cross-frame dependencies. Together, these components preserve fidelity, enhance fine-grained realism, and maintain temporal consistency. Extensive experiments show that our method substantially outperforms existing video restoration approaches in visual quality, detail richness, and temporal stability.

abstract: Predicting ammonia (NH3) concentrations during aerobic chicken manure composting provides critical feedforward signals for intelligent aeration. However, the concurrence of long-term biochemical evolution and intermittent forced-aeration pulses poses significant modeling hurdles across steady baselines, transient surges, and risk quantification. Existing data-driven models lack physical consistency, while mechanistic kinetic models struggle with environmental disturbances. To bridge this gap, we propose PINN-PatchTST-GPR, a physics-informed neuro-symbolic forecasting framework. Validated on a 28-day composting campaign across six vertical bioreactors, the framework couples a channel-independent PatchTST backbone with macroscopic kinetic constraints, dynamic physical bounds, and a Gaussian process regression (GPR) event specialist. Multi-channel sensor streams drive discrete differential equation residuals and non-negativity bounds, strictly ensuring physical plausibility. A block-split conformal prediction module yields nominal 90% distribution-free prediction intervals, while PySINDy and PySR extract low-complexity symbolic equations for quiescent and surge regimes. The model achieves an overall RMSE of 0.8256 +/- 0.0132 ppm, R2 of 0.9817 +/- 0.0006, Epeak of 1.6793 +/- 0.0725 ppm, and Etime of 0.7 +/- 0.2 min. For uncertainty quantification, it attains PICP90 of 99.792 +/- 0.047%, MPIW of 6.951 +/- 0.128 ppm, and IS0.1 of 6.968 +/- 0.128 ppm. Symbolically, PySINDy yields an RMSE of 0.4624 +/- 0.0758 ppm (R2 = 0.9896), while PySR yields 2.4084 +/- 0.0864 ppm (R2 = 0.9523). Biologically, the 20-min aeration strategy minimizes cumulative NH3 emissions. Overall, PINN-PatchTST-GPR harmonizes global forecasting, localized transient responsiveness, and risk quantification for precision composting.

abstract: Large language models with retrieval-augmented generation systematically underutilize evidence in the middle of multi-document contexts, a phenomenon known as Lost in the Middle. Existing mitigation strategies, such as document reordering and attention steering, can reduce boundary bias but remain brittle in noisy settings, where inaccurate relevance estimation and spurious documents still obscure useful evidence in central positions. We propose DuQUAD, a multi-document QA framework that mitigates positional bias through dual-view reasoning and quality-aware evidence pruning. DuQUAD combines a Local Agent guided by a Structural Fusion Score with a Global Agent that reasons over the full document set, providing both targeted evidence recovery and broad contextual understanding. The framework further filters candidate evidence using explicit quality scoring and refines it at the sentence level to reduce noise. DuQUAD consistently outperforms strong Lost-in-the-Middle mitigation baselines, including hybrid retrieval and reranking, multi-agent reasoning, and context optimization methods, improving accuracy by 3.0% on average over the strongest competing baseline and gold evidence recall by 9.4%, while substantially reducing computational cost compared to existing multi-agent frameworks.

abstract: The aquaculture industry needs to address several challenges to secure sustainable seafood production that can serve an increasing global demand. One major challenge is to ensure good fish health and acceptable welfare during production since the improvement of fish welfare is of vital importance in current and future production systems. In this study, this is addressed by developing and implementing methods to identify fish behaviors in response to intrusive objects both on individual and on a group basis. A novel approach for detecting, tracking, and estimating the 3D position of individual fish has thus been developed, and specifically designed to track the caudal fins of farmed fish in industrial sea cages. The tracking data was subjected to a novel stereo-vision method adapted to estimate fish positions, velocities, accelerations, and turning and pitch angles. Datasets obtained from industrial-scale fish farms were then analyzed to identify the impact of structures of varying shapes, sizes, and colors on fish behavior. The method was trained using manually labeled caudal fins, and used YOLOv8 with ByteTrack as an object detector and tracker, SuperGlue for matching detections in the left and right frames, and triangulation to reconstruct the 3D positions of the fish. Different image pre-processing and augmentation methods for enhancing object detection accuracy were tested and their performance compared, while RAFT-Stereo was tested for depth estimation purposes. The obtained results both validate the method's performance against previous research efforts, and demonstrate the novelty and potential of this method in providing more insight into behavioral dynamics in sea-cages.

abstract: Higher education is confronting an academic-integrity challenge unlike any in its history. Students can now outsource homework, take-home assignments, and online examinations to large language models (LLMs) that complete them in seconds. Existing research on evaluating LLM performance on academic assessments has focused largely on standardized examinations, or on questions from college-level courses drawn from a single discipline. Far less is known about how LLMs perform on college-level assessment questions spanning multiple disciplines, that instructors have purposely designed to be AI-resistant, and about which features of such questions, if any, meaningfully constrain LLM performance. We address this gap by collecting 75 questions from authentic college coursework assessments, spanning 17 disciplines, which were contributed by 37 faculty members from ten U.S. universities and one U.K. university. Of these, 61 questions were intentionally designed by faculty members to be 'LLM-proof', while the remaining 14 questions were sourced from online courses. We then (i) evaluate three state-of-the-art LLMs' ability to correctly answer these questions with and without supplementary course materials; (ii) identify five strategies, through thematic analysis, that faculty used to make their questions harder for LLMs to solve; and (iii) test whether these strategies impact LLMs' ability to answer the questions accurately. Our experimental results show that the best-performing model scored approximately 83% without supplementary course materials and 85% with them, and we observed noteworthy differences across models, answer formats, and instructor tweaking strategies. We discuss implications for assessment design, academic-integrity policy, and the broader ethics of deploying LLMs in educational settings.

abstract: Collecting demonstrations for bimanual dexterous manipulation is costly, motivating the use of human videos as a source of robot training data. However, uncertainty in video-derived motion estimates and differences between human and robot embodiments make direct motion transfer challenging. In this work, we introduce PriDex, a framework that transforms human-video Priors into executable robot Dexterous manipulation demonstrations through reinforcement learning in simulation. PriDex preserves task-relevant interaction structure while allowing embodiment-specific behavior to be regenerated for the robot. Human-object interactions provide affordance cues for selecting task-relevant, robot-specific grasps from geometry-based candidates. For motion refinement, object trajectories provide a task-level reference, while relative bimanual wrist trajectories offer complementary guidance for coordinated motion. Since object-motion estimates can become unreliable under occlusion or visual ambiguity, PriDex uses object-motion confidence to adaptively balance these two priors, emphasizing object-level guidance when confidence is high and increasing the contribution of wrist-level guidance as confidence decreases. Reinforcement learning refines these video-derived priors under the robot's kinematic and physical constraints, and the resulting policies are rolled out to generate robot demonstrations for training a vision-based diffusion policy. abstract: Sequential recommenders can generate synthetic interaction sequences and retrain on the augmented corpus in a recursive self-improvement loop. To limit error accumulation, current methods verify each generated sequence remains predictive of the user's real interactions and discard those that drift away from it. Verification does not, however, determine which verified sequences should train the next model. With every verified sequence used for training, source sequences yielding more verified sequences or longer continuations have more influence, although neither quantity indicates how much those sequences will help the next model. We formulate the decision of which verified sequences are used to train the next model as \emph{post-verification acquisition} and introduce {\bf Disagreement-Aware Recursive Self-Improving Recommendation (DA-RSIR)}. DA-RSIR caps each source sequence's contribution and ranks its verified sequences by how much the model's predictions disagree over their augmented interactions. It uses a score derived from Bayesian Active Learning by Disagreement (BALD) and estimated with Monte Carlo (MC) dropout. DA-RSIR requires no extra labels, teacher model, or quality scorer. Across four datasets, three recommender models, and two metrics, it improves on the retain-all approach in all $24$ comparisons and attains the highest mean in $23$ of $24$ overall; the aggregate improvement is statistically significant on both metrics. A single DA-RSIR round exceeds the retain-all approach's best gain over five recursive rounds. These findings establish post-verification acquisition as a separate control point in recursive self-improvement, separating which sequences pass verification from which verified sequences are used to train the next model.

abstract: Early substance use initiation is associated with later substance use disorders, but the relative contributions of environmental, behavioral, and genetic factors during adolescence remain unclear. We analyzed 2,366 participants of European genetic ancestry from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study. Four outcomes were examined through four years of follow-up: initiation of alcohol, nicotine, cannabis, and any substance use. Time-varying Cox models screened predictors, followed by LASSO-selected multivariable Cox models adjusted for age, sex, ancestry principal components, and study site. Marginal structural models evaluated selected predictors. Environmental and behavioral factors were the strongest and most consistent predictors, including youth rule-breaking, impulsivity, parental alcohol-related problems, financial adversity, family context, phone use, negative life events, peer or romantic experiences, sleep, caffeine exposure, and parental monitoring. Polygenic risk scores for alcohol, cannabis, nicotine, and substance use disorder showed weaker and less consistent associations. Although some appeared in screening models, none remained robust after correction, multivariable selection, or causal modeling. In marginal structural models, youth rule-breaking was consistently associated with all four outcomes. Other outcome-specific signals included sensation seeking, lack of planning, parental alcohol-related problems, phone use, sleep duration, and parental monitoring. Early substance use initiation was more strongly associated with dynamic environmental, behavioral, family, and psychosocial factors than with common-variant genetic liability. These findings highlight modifiable developmental pathways and support prevention strategies focused on proximal behavioral and environmental risk contexts.

abstract: Multimodal Emotion Recognition in Conversation (MERC) combines lexical, acoustic, visual and conversational cues, but accepting audio and video does not establish their effective or robust use. We audit off-the-shelf Omni models while holding the target transcript and prior textual context fixed and adding, removing or replacing target audio and video. In the primary evaluation of Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, Baichuan-Omni-1.5 and MiniCPM-o 2.6 on MELD and the full five-session six-class IEMOCAP set, T+A improves Accuracy in all six model-dataset pairs, with four gains significant after false discovery rate (FDR) correction. Across three source mappings, unrelated A/V (RandA/V) lowers Accuracy relative to Full in all 18 comparisons; all 18 remain significant under dialogue-cluster inference and BH-FDR correction, both on common-valid pairs and when invalid/OOM outcomes are treated as incorrect. Comparisons with modality-omission baselines further distinguish replacement penalties from mismatch-specific harm. A Qwen/MELD case study finds significantly greater gold-vs-best-candidate margin recovery in Late than Early or Middle under decision-query audio knockout, relative to an edge-count-matched Video-Sham control, using Holm-corrected tests. These results distinguish genuine-modality benefit from sensitivity and vulnerability to misleading input.

abstract: Industrial anomaly detection plays a pivotal role in precision manufacturing, where joint analysis of multimodal data emerges as a critical approach to enhance detection accuracy. Feature reconstruction, a dominant paradigm for such joint analysis, is primarily implemented through intra-modal and cross-modal methods, both of which are plagued by significant limitations. Intra-modal reconstruction neglects complementary cross-modal information, while its cross-modal counterpart is prone to projection errors and ambiguous one-to-many mappings (e.g., same textures mapping to multiple geometries), leading to detection failures. To address these limitations, we propose a novel feature reconstruction paradigm, Fuse Before Reconstruct (FBR), which first fuses multimodal features and then performs reconstruction for anomaly detection. Firstly, we propose a bidirectional cross-modal attention mechanism to achieve deep feature complementarity between image and point cloud features, mitigating projection bias through channel alignment and dynamic spatial prior integration. Besides, a learnable pixel-wise gated fusion strategy is adopted to preserve multi-modal structural consistency while optimizing local feature combination. Finally, dual-path collaborative reconstruction is implemented to recover original modal features from the fused representations, where cross-modal consistency constraints effectively eliminate mapping ambiguities. Extensive experiments show that FBR achieves 98.3% I-AUROC on MVTec 3D-AD and 92.6% I-AUROC on Eyecandies, surpassing previous state-of-the-art methods by +2.9% and +4.1%, respectively.

abstract: Muon is a stochastic first-order optimizer for matrix-valued parameters. It maintains an exponential moving average of stochastic gradients in a momentum buffer with coefficient $β$, and orthogonalizes the buffer to obtain the update direction. Muon has been reported to accelerate and stabilize the training of large language models. In practice, it is often used with shuffling (sampling without replacement), where each epoch visits the components of a finite-sum objective in a permuted order. However, its iteration complexity in this setting remains open. We analyze Muon under shuffling, with the momentum buffer orthogonalized by the polar map. For smooth nonconvex finite-sum problems, we establish an $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-3})$ iteration complexity for finding an $\varepsilon$-stationary point. This guarantee holds for every sequence of permutations, covering random reshuffling, shuffle once, and the incremental gradient method. This complexity matches that of stochastic gradient descent under shuffling in its dependence on $\varepsilon$, and improves on Muon's $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-4})$ complexity under sampling with replacement. Our guarantee requires a problem-dependent $β$ that approaches one as the number of components grows. In contrast, no fixed $β$ guarantees convergence to stationarity for every number of components. We show this by constructing a family of smooth convex problems on which, for any fixed $β\in[0,1)$, Muon remains bounded away from stationarity once the number of components is sufficiently large. This failure occurs for every sequence of permutations and persists even with small stepsizes. These results suggest two practical tuning rules: if the training loss stops decreasing even after reducing the stepsize, increase $β$; when increasing $β$, reduce the stepsize accordingly.

abstract: Industrial systems continuously generate time series that vary in sampling frequency, scale, dynamics, and operating regime. Consequently a single time-series foundation model may not be able to represent all regimes effectively and retraining a large model for every new dataset or regime shift is computationally expensive. Modular foundation models address this issue by reusing specialised encoders trained on diverse datasets and by allowing the expansion of capabilities through the addition of new experts. This approach requires compact experts to minimize storage cost and a proper selection mechanism of experts for unseen data. We propose a modular foundation model framework that combines end-to-end Bayesian encoder training with uncertainty based routing. Using Singular Bayesian Neural Networks (SBNNs), we build a collection of compact Bayesian encoders whose epistemic uncertainty guides label-free selection. At the selected ranks, our Bayesian collection uses 63.8\% less storage than its deterministic counterpart. We evaluate this framework on time-series data through distribution shift, encoder selection, and probabilistic forecasting. Across seven incoming datasets, uncertainty-based routing is competitive with distance-based routing in terms of forecast MSE, while reducing average ECE from 0.086 to 0.072 and average NLL from 0.907 to 0.836. It also increases PICP90 from 82.28\% to 89.03\%. In a separate model-family comparison, we evaluate the SBNN pipeline against full-rank Bayes by Backprop, deep ensembles, and MC Dropout. The SBNN pipeline achieves an average MSE of 0.390, comparable with 0.396 for deep ensembles, 0.389 for MC dropout, and 0.443 for the full-rank Bayesian model. It uses 63.9\% fewer parameters than MC dropout, 81.9\% fewer than the full-rank model, and 92.8\% fewer than the deep ensemble.

abstract: As social and service robots increasingly share interaction spaces in public, they may form groups while coordinating tasks or interacting with humans. Initial group formation alone is insufficient in dynamic settings, because it can be disrupted when a person or another agent joins, leaves, or passes through the group. Although group dynamics and repositioning have been widely studied in swarm robotics and virtual-agent settings, little attention has been given to socially appropriate repositioning behaviors in groups of humanoid robots. Existing social-force-based approaches provide a useful foundation for group behavior, but they have limited obstacle handling, and can produce unsafe behavior as environmental complexity increases. We propose a novel framework that modulates traditional Social Force, guided by Model Predictive Control (MPC) to plan ahead, bounded by Control Barrier Functions (CBF) to increase safety for robot groups repositioning behaviors. This approach aims to produce safer and socially aware group repositioning behaviors under various group formation disturbance. We evaluate the method in simulation through an ablation study and an online user study. The results show that our proposed method can produce smoother and safer repositioning behaviors in complex environments while preserving social appropriateness.

abstract: We study the design of priority pricing systems with heterogeneous agents in environments in which improving quality for some agents reduces the average quality that can be provided. Contrary to the equity-efficiency tradeoff emphasized in public debates, we show that under economically natural conditions priority pricing can Pareto-improve on an equal-allocation benchmark. Three priority tiers suffice for such an improvement, combining higher quality for a fee, lower quality with compensation, and an intermediate tier at the benchmark quality; two tiers are never enough. Our results provide a framework for overcoming equity-efficiency tensions in applications such as lane pricing, waiting-line design, public provision, and insurance.

abstract: Reliable protection under varying power system operating conditions requires rapid fault detection while preserving selectivity against external faults and non-fault disturbances. This requirement is particularly challenging in communication-free schemes, where relays must determine trip conditions solely from local electrical measurements. To address this challenge, this paper proposes a directionally supervised neuromorphic protection scheme that integrates disturbance-responsive leaky integrate-and-fire dynamics with a direction-dependent firing threshold to distinguish internal faults from reverse-direction events. The unified relay architecture combines local disturbance detection, directional discrimination, and spike-based trip generation without requiring inter-relay communication. Its performance is evaluated under grid-connected and islanded conditions using a ring microgrid and the IEEE 13-node distribution feeder. Across 240 evaluated fault scenarios, the framework achieves median operating times of 5.4--7.6 ms across the two networks, with 78% of cases operating within 10 ms and 95% within 20 ms. It also maintains protection security during load disturbances, while fault-resistance analysis confirms its response under high-resistance faults. Controller-hardware-in-the-loop (CHIL) experiments using an RTDS simulator and an external dSPACE controller demonstrate trip-command assertion in approximately 10 ms and 5 ms for the tested single-line-to-ground and three-phase-to-ground faults, respectively. The results establish real-time feasibility within the evaluated conditions and characterize operating-time variability across fault types and resistance levels for different network configurations.

abstract: Foundation models produce high-dimensional latent representations in which suitably designed statistical decision rules can be effective yet analytically tractable. We study such detectors in the high-dimensional regime, where latent dimension and training sample size grow proportionally. For linear and quadratic statistics, we derive explicit large-deviation characterizations of false-alarm and miss-detection performance under the Neyman-Pearson paradigm, and show how the binary analysis extends to multi-class classification. The resulting error probabilities and corresponding decay rates exhibit non-monotonic dependence on the shape parameter, including double-descent and, in some regimes, multiple-descent. Experiments on vision, text, and audio datasets using modern foundation models show close agreement between theoretical predictions and empirical performance. In particular, the proposed framework allows us to set a prescribed false-alarm level and accurately predict the corresponding miss-detection probability. Overall, our results provide a theoretically grounded and interpretable framework with competitive empirical performance across different modalities.

abstract: Off-policy evaluation (OPE) is essential for assessing decision policies before deployment when online experimentation is costly or unsafe. Accurate estimation remains difficult when behavior-policy data are limited and the target policy favors states and actions rarely observed in those data. We propose InCOPE, a prior-data fitted network that learns a shared policy-value prediction rule across synthetic OPE tasks. We construct an OPE task prior over Markov decision processes and behavior-target policy pairs, generating behavior-policy datasets and exact target-policy values for pretraining. For a new tabular decision problem, the pretrained network uses the behavior-policy dataset, target policy, and known task settings as context to predict the policy's expected return without task-specific parameter updates. Experiments across four tabular domains, including a semi-synthetic clinical setting, demonstrate InCOPE's effectiveness for policy-value estimation.

abstract: Objectives: To measure whether a locally hosted large language model (LLM), stacked with deterministic and clinical named-entity recognition (NER) detectors, finds more protected health information (PHI) than open tools, and at what precision. Materials and Methods: DeidSharp, an open-source .NET toolkit, combines the findings of pluggable detectors (patterns, a clinical NER model, a local 26B mixture-of-experts LLM) and fails closed on any detector error. Configurations fixed on tuning halves were compared, under a prespecified protocol, with deid, Philter, the Stanford/Penn de-identifier, OpenAI Privacy Filter and GLiNER on reporting halves of PhysioNet's nursing notes (889 spans) and semi-synthetic MIMIC-IV-Note discharge summaries (29,023 spans), and on synthetic ASQ-PHI queries, with paired patient-level bootstrap intervals. Results: In the nursing notes, against Stanford/Penn, the recall-first stack found 98.9% of PHI (+2.8, 95% CI 1.4 to 4.4) at 9.3 points lower precision; the precision-first stack, without NER, found 96.5%, matching Stanford/Penn, at 19.6 points higher precision (83.2%). In the discharge summaries, both stacks led Stanford/Penn by more than 20 points (recall-first 95.3%, +21.5, 20.5 to 22.4), almost entirely on generated untyped names; on typed labels all three exceeded 99%. All four prespecified comparisons held. No configuration beat deid significantly on its home corpus; Philter found more discharge-summary spans than the recall-first stack at 23 points lower precision. Discussion: The LLM was the main detector and NER added place names; asked to verify its own findings, the LLM discarded a quarter of true PHI. Conclusion: A local LLM layered with deterministic detectors offers recall-first and precision-first operating points without sending text off-site.

abstract: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations can capture the nanoscale physics of fracture at the atomistic level, but their computational cost prohibits predictions at the length scales and time scales needed for many applications. Machine learning approaches, on the other hand, have been proposed as heuristic surrogates for material fracture, yet they cannot guarantee the physical consistency of the predicted response. To address this shortcoming, we propose the mesoscale neural operator (MNO): a data-driven nonlocal constitutive model that is learned directly from MD loading and displacement data. After training, it can be used in continuum fracture simulations on much larger domains and grid sizes. The key idea of the MNO is to exploit the built-in characteristic length of a nonlocal model, called the horizon, to travel across scales. Physical consistency across scales is obtained by building two structural ingredients into the MNO: a normalized kernel that renders the strain energy density invariant under horizon rescaling, and a rescaled critical bond stretch that keeps the energy release rate consistent across scales. abstract: Clinical dietary assessment can generate detailed but high-dimensional nutrient and food-group information that is difficult to translate quickly into counselling priorities. This paper proposes an explainable unsupervised-to-supervised machine learning framework for discovering, reproducing and interpreting dietary patterns using public UK National Diet and Nutrition Survey data. Adult participants aged 19 years and above from NDNS Years 12-15 were represented using 25 energy-adjusted nutrient and food-group features. K-means, Gaussian Mixture Models and Agglomerative Clustering were compared across k = 2-8, with stability and dietetic interpretability used alongside internal validation metrics. The selected K-means k = 4 solution identified four interpretable dietary patterns: high fat/meat and sodium, higher fibre fruit-vegetable micronutrient, high free-sugar snacks and sugary drinks, and dairy/cereal calcium-rich saturated-fat. A supervised surrogate classifier reproduced held-out cluster membership with high test performance (macro-F1 = 0.963), but was interpreted only as an explanatory surrogate rather than as an independent clinical prediction model. SHAP analysis linked predictions to dietetically meaningful drivers, suggesting potential value for dietitian-in-the-loop assessment, counselling prioritisation and follow-up monitoring.

abstract: We provide a uniform guarantee for a continuous-review lost-sales inventory system with unit Poisson demand, deterministic lead time, and fixed ordering costs: a simple algorithm computes an $(r,Q)$ policy and chooses between that policy and no replenishment, with cost at most $(\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{6})/2<1.932$ times the unrestricted nonanticipative optimum. The algorithm starts by generating an optimal integer base-stock policy, which at zero setup cost achieves the tight worst-case factor $\sqrt{2}$ relative to the optimal system cost. For positive setup costs, it uses the reorder point of this integer base-stock policy and an integer lot at the economic order quantity scale. The inclusion of ordinary base stock in the continuous-review capped base-stock family also improves that family's earlier asymptotic $1.79$ upper guarantee to a uniform $\sqrt{2}$ guarantee valid at every finite parameter vector. To establish these guarantees, we construct a computable lower bound on the zero-setup optimal cost by tracking units already on hand or committed for delivery. We then combine it with a bound on holding and setup costs required by batching to obtain the general-setup guarantee and instance-specific performance bounds for any admissible replenishment policy. In our numerical study, the largest estimated policy-cost-to-lower-bound ratios are about $1.59$ for our heuristic $(r, Q)$ policy and $1.47$ after joint optimization of $r$ and $Q$. The heuristic also performs well against the optimized policy: over the sampled instances, its median extra cost ranges from $2.33\%$ to $3.91\%$, depending on the setup cost.

abstract: Rigorous economic models can take months to construct, yet energy crises demand decisions from policymakers within days or even hours. Any disruption in energy markets is not isolated but rapidly disseminates through interlinked global systems. Off-the-shelf models that already exist typically focus only on limited aspects of the system and are distributed across research groups, programming languages, software architectures not designed for model integration, and incompatible formats. Integrating these models manually can take longer than the crisis itself, forcing analysts to rely on whichever models are easiest to connect and leaving consequential scenarios unexplored. Policymakers must make rapid decisions with obstructed and limited information. We show that large language models can perform the critical integration directly. The system constructs internally consistent scenarios, translates assumptions into model-specific inputs, executes existing economic and physical models in dependency order, and synthesizes outputs tailored to policymakers. The language model generates no quantitative results: every reported value is reproduced directly from an underlying model run, remains traceable to its source and is subject to analyst approval at each stage. We develop a LLM framework that coordinates 16 models of oil, natural gas, shipping, water, helium, fertilizer and macroeconomic equilibrium. The framework is applied across five scenarios to assess the 2026 closure of the Strait of Hormuz and refreshed weekly for eight weeks as events on the ground continued to unfold. By linking models that already exist and reading them as a suite rather than in isolation, this architecture mobilizes distributed scientific models rapidly during energy and geopolitical disruptions while keeping any single model's assumptions from driving the conclusion.

abstract: Language models are now a standard tool for measuring what managers say on earnings calls, but the encoders behind these measures were usually pretrained on text from the same years a backtest covers. Holding out a test period does not remove that hindsight, because it sits in the features. We adapt NoLBERT, an encoder pretrained only on text published between 1976 and 1995, to earnings calls without letting it read anything dated after 31 December 2023. The calls supply the training signal themselves: every analyst question is followed by management's answer, and the model learns to pick that answer out from the other answers of the same call. We test on every US call from January 2025 to October 2026 (20,323 calls, 254,575 questions) and make every modeling choice on calls from 2024. The adapted model, NoLBERT-Calls-2023, ranks the true answer first for 78.0% of questions (95% interval 77.8-78.2; chance 8.0%), against 26.3% before adaptation. It is 1.0 point ahead of a call-adapted ChronoBERT, 3.4 points ahead of a call-adapted FinBERT, and 18.7 and 19.8 points ahead of the best off-the-shelf retriever and BM25. A year-by-year test over 2013-2026 finds no look-ahead premium: relative to a model adapted only through 2012, the released model does no better on the years it was trained on than on years it never saw. The price of the cutoff is compute: under one shared 150-minute recipe NoLBERT adapts least well of four encoders, and its lead comes from a longer, staged adaptation of about 13 GPU-hours.

abstract: Must a detector see generated images in order to catch them? Detection of AI-generated images has long faced two problems. The cues a detector learns from the few generators in its training set carry traces specific to those generators and transfer poorly to new ones, which limits generalization. The real and generated training images also differ in format and content, so the detector takes these differences as evidence of authenticity, and its decisions change with factors that have nothing to do with authenticity, which harms robustness as well as generalization. Both problems stem from training on generated images. A detector never trained on them can largely avoid both at the source. Vision foundation models have already learned the concept of "AI-generated" during pretraining, and text can point to it directly. Building on this, we propose SaySee, a training-free detector: Say builds a generation direction from sets of paired descriptions that differ only in authenticity and scores an image by the projection of its embedding onto it, and See uses real images to correct the score offsets caused by format, image type and content. On 24 evaluation sets that span standard benchmarks, in-the-wild data and the latest generators, SaySee reaches a mean AUC of 98.2% with MoE-ViE, 4.2 points above the best existing detector. When format is decoupled from authenticity, it remains the best of all methods. Code will be released.

abstract: Embodied capabilities such as visual grounding, spatial reasoning, navigation, and driving understanding are often developed in separate vision-language specialists fine-tuned from a common pretrained model.Deploying the specialists separately multiplies storage, whereas merging them into one dense model forces conflicting task updates to share parameters and loses part of each specialist's expertise.We introduce UNITE, a framework that consolidates such specialists into a compact shared-backbone mixture of experts. UNITE keeps the feed-forward block of each specialist as a routable expert and represents the expert bank through a shared-anchor one-bit factorization: a shared floating-point anchor plus expert-specific, row-scaled binary deviations.The anchor is optimized jointly with the scales and signs through closed-form alternating updates, using only source weights and no calibration data.Router adaptation then adjusts token-level expert selection with the backbone and experts frozen, updating fewer than $0.6$M parameters ($<0.01\%$ of the $8.8$B active parameters). Built from four Qwen3-VL-8B specialists, the complete UNITE model occupies $20.3$ GB, $1.16\times$ the storage of one dense specialist and $59.6\%$ below the uncompressed MoE. Across $22$ benchmarks and R2R Val-Unseen, UNITE matches six static merging methods in mean retention of best-specialist performance, leads all of them on Scan2Cap, ScanQA, and all four navigation metrics, and surpasses every source specialist on all five 3D scene understanding benchmarks (up to $+19.1$ on Scan2Cap) and on R2R navigation. Relative to the uncompressed MoE, factorization is nearly lossless on $21$ of $22$ benchmarks; the exception is VSI-Bench, where frame-count experiments suggest impaired use of cross-frame evidence.UNITE thus consolidates complementary embodied capabilities near single-model storage.

abstract: I measure whether the rise of services is ultimately supported by household consumption or by non-household demand through production networks, investment, exports, and government. Using harmonized input-output tables for 76 economies over 1995-2022, I attribute service value added to its ultimate domestic final-demand category and measure the household orientation of each service economy in both levels and growth. The conventional service share does not reveal the type: it is negatively correlated with household orientation, and only about four in ten tertiarization episodes are majority-household. Among the 65 economies whose service share rose over 1995-2018, 77 percent became less household-oriented; the share is 75 percent under a two-percentage-point material-change threshold. Yet household-supported production becomes more service-intensive with income because households' aggregate position falls faster. A one-type benchmark has no purchaser margin; a two-type extension gives the condition for this reversal. An exact Leontief accounting and Shapley decomposition allocate a median 73 percent of service-share growth to production-system channels, which are the largest contribution in 80 percent of economies with materially rising shares. The decline in household orientation is instead allocated mainly to aggregate final-demand structure. The service share records how much service activity exists, not which economic transformation produced it.

abstract: Model compression can facilitate the deployment of large language models in resource-constrained legal settings, but its effects on domain-specific performance may depend on the evaluation protocol. We investigate this issue using ArabLegalEval, a Saudi Arabic legal benchmark, under both with-context and no-context evaluation. The former provides supporting legal passages, while the latter assesses performance without external context. Removing the context produces accuracy gaps of up to 27 percentage points for the base model. We examine three stages: domain adaptation, quantization, and knowledge distillation across FANAR-9B, JAIS-8B, and Qwen2.5-7B. Four-bit quantization reduces model memory by 64-71%, with changes in no-context MCQ accuracy ranging from -3.2 to +1.6 percentage points. Distillation produces more variable results, with accuracy generally declining as student size decreases. A Qwen2.5-7B student distilled from FANAR achieves 76.6% no-context accuracy, compared with 77.2% for its teacher. Our findings suggest that no-context evaluation provides a useful complement to context-supported testing when assessing the effects of adaptation and compression on Arabic legal language models.

abstract: Many manipulation tasks require separating adhered, embedded, contaminated, or mechanically constrained targets. We study this setting as removal manipulation, where progress depends on evolving contact states that are only partially observable from vision and kinematics. We introduce DexRemo, a three-finger robotic hand with high-force actuation, modular fingertips, and three-axis fingertip force sensing, together with a nine-scenario real-robot task suite spanning adhesive detachment, surface cleaning and self-cleaning, and occluded retrieval. To make multi-finger force observations easier to fuse, we express fingertip forces in a shared wrist-centered frame, giving force components consistent geometric meaning across fingers and time. Using an Action Chunking Transformer backbone, policies fuse multi-view vision, proprioception, fingertip pose, and force observations to predict closed-loop action chunks from demonstrations. Evaluation uses six core benchmark tasks for controlled fingertip-input and force-frame ablations, plus three extension scenarios for additional held-out coverage. Across these evaluations, the learned policies achieve consistent removal performance, and ablations show that wrist-frame forces, especially with fingertip pose, improve stability and generalization over local-frame force inputs and no-force baselines. Project website: https://dexremo.github.io

abstract: Neural-network approximations of nonlinear model predictive control can reduce online computational costs, but ensuring constraint satisfaction and closed-loop stability remains challenging. We propose a framework in which convex optimisation is used to restore feasibility under suitable local assumptions, while bounds on the corrected controller's cost suboptimality provide sufficient conditions for practical closed-loop stability. To assess these conditions over a compact set of initial states, we investigate a branch-and-bound approach based on convex relaxations of the nonlinear dynamics, with probabilistic guarantees established through scenario optimisation. The proposed approach represents a step towards combining the computational efficiency of approximate nonlinear model predictive control with systematic methods for restoring feasibility and assessing stability.

abstract: Labelling tissue components in histology whole slide images (WSIs) is prohibitively labour-intensive: a single slide may contain tens of thousands of structures--cells, nuclei, and other morphologically distinct objects--each requiring manual boundary delineation and classification. We present a cloudnative, end-to-end pipeline that automates this process through a cluster-first paradigm. Our system tiles WSIs, filters out tiles deemed unlikely to contain valuable information, segments tissue components with Cellpose-SAM (including cells, nuclei, and other morphologically similar structures), extracts neural embeddings via a pretrained ResNet-50, reduces dimensionality with UMAP, and groups morphologically similar objects using DBSCAN clustering. Under this paradigm, a human annotator labels representative clusters rather than individual objects, reducing annotation effort by orders of magnitude. We evaluate the pipeline on 3,696 tissue components across 13 diverse tissue types from three species (human, rat, rabbit), measuring how well unsupervised clusters align with independent human labels via per-tile Hungarian-algorithm matching. Our system achieves a weighted cluster-label alignment accuracy of 96.8%, with 7 of 13 tissue types reaching perfect agreement. The pipeline, a companion labelling web application, and all evaluation code are released as open-source software.

abstract: Global minimization of multivariate polynomials is computationally difficult in general, and nonnegativity does not necessarily imply a sum-of-squares (SoS) representation. We show that adding sufficiently strong Euclidean regularization to a polynomial provides a general mechanism for overcoming such challenges. Namely, for any multivariate polynomial $P$ of degree at most $p$ with a nonzero linear coefficient, and any even integer $2d>p$, we prove that $m_σ(s)=P(s)+\fracσ{2d}\|s\|_2^{2d}$ is SoS exact for all sufficiently large $σ$. Furthermore, the shifted polynomial $m_σ-\min m_σ$ admits a positive-definite Gram representation on appropriately-shifted nonconstant monomials. Consequently, the global minimum and minimizer can be recovered exactly by a single degree-$d$ semidefinite programming (SDP) representation, whose size is polynomial in the dimension for fixed $d$, without requiring higher levels of the SoS hierarchy. The proof develops a degree-independent mechanism based on the Bregman remainder of the regularizer: its strict Gram margin absorbs the lower-degree polynomial perturbations. We further establish an analogous exact SDP regime for polynomial optimization over sufficiently small Euclidean balls, connecting large regularization with small-radius trust-region problems. Finally, we investigate how the algebraic structure of the regularizer governs the existence of a strict Gram margin, extending the mechanism beyond Euclidean norms while identifying limitations of coordinate-separable regularization.

abstract: Deep models often rely on spurious correlations that fail on underrepresented groups. Existing methods either correct human-specified bias attributes or infer unknown biases from the learned representation space. However, annotated attributes may differ from the shortcuts actually used by a model, while a single representation provides incomplete and potentially noisy evidence. Our key insight is that a bias obscured in one feature space may be clearer in another. In this work, we propose CHORD (Cross-view Harmonic Outlier Reversal for Debiasing), a multi-view framework that allows samples to "sing in chorus" across diverse representation spaces to achieve robust cross-view consensus. CHORD aggregates aggregates within-class partitions in each view, which is a proxy for specifying candidate biases, to debias the target representation and classifier without bias supervision. abstract: We present recent developments in Halpern Peaceman-Rachford (HPR) methods for solving large-scale linear programming problems. We first introduce the semi-proximal HPR framework and summarize its convergence guarantees, together with its connections to Halpern PDHG and ergodic Peaceman-Rachford iterations. To improve practical performance, we develop adaptive restart and penalty parameter update strategies. We then describe several computational enhancements, including GPU-based preprocessing, diagonal scaling, reusable execution plans for sparse matrix-vector multiplication, and sieving techniques. We further discuss multi-GPU parallelization and lossless model storage and loading for handling large-scale instances. These developments form the foundation of HPR-LP, a GPU-accelerated solver for large-scale linear programming.

abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can correctly interpret physics diagrams yet apply constraints outside the states or conditions in which they hold, causing premise errors to propagate through subsequent calculations. We introduce PhysScope, an inference-time visual harness that supports self-correction of these scope mismatches without updating model weights. PhysScope enables the model to link physical scopes directly to its visual observations and explicitly constructs derived views to support reasoning. The harness imposes explicit constraints on state distinctions, conditions, and physical scopes during model reasoning, and checks agent-proposed revisions against sources and scopes. Accepted revisions invalidate registered dependents, thereby maintaining scope-aware working memory. On PhysAlign, PhysScope achieves higher solving scores than direct solving across all six evaluated VLMs. With Gemini-3.8-flash, it outperforms Canvas-CoT by 9.34 percentage points and substantially improves solving accuracy on the out-of-distribution (OOD) PhysUniBench benchmark. Ablation studies support explicit scope management and dependency maintenance as design principles for multimodal physics reasoning agents.

abstract: In mineral exploration, verifying geological hypotheses relies on designing a variety of geochemical experiments. While large language model (LLM) agents increasingly automate downstream geoscientific data analysis, a crucial upstream capability remains largely unexplored: automated geochemical experimental design, i.e., deciding which experiments to conduct before committing to costly laboratory work. Evaluating this capability of LLM agents is difficult for two reasons. First, geochemical experiments exhibit high methodological diversity and subjectivity: to test the same hypothesis, different geologists may choose different minerals and instruments, so no single protocol can serve as the reference answer. Second, open-ended experimental plans resist representation as structured labels, which makes objective scoring difficult. To address these challenges, we introduce MineralExp, a benchmark that reformulates geochemical experimental design as a hypothesis-based experiment selection problem, i.e., a multi-label classification problem. We abstract concrete instrument names and procedural details into a shared taxonomy of 19 experimental types across five mineral-system processes: Source, Transport, Deposition, Modification, and Preservation. This taxonomy yields deterministic multi-label targets while accommodating diverse experimental protocols. Constructed from published ore-deposit literature and verified by domain experts, MineralExp comprises 277 cases and 1,572 reference experimental plans. Given a geological hypothesis and initial context, an LLM agent selects the relevant tasks and generates concrete experimental plans, which are scored by multi-label classification metrics and an LLM-as-a-Judge metric. The experimental results show that current agents generally achieve high recall but low precision, tending to propose more experiments than are necessary to test the hypothesis.

abstract: A fixed number of recent observations may span minutes for one variable and days for another. Earlier measurements can still reveal whether the latest value is unusual for that variable. We propose TRESS (Timestamped Recent Events and Statistical Summaries), a forecasting model that retains the latest observations at their original times and summarises the full history of each variable. For a given set of variables and event budget, this representation stays the same size as the record grows. Its query-conditioned event lifting module weights deviations from the latest value according to the age of each observation and the forecast horizon. A channel-specific decoder combines the resulting features with historical statistics and a summary shared across variables to predict a correction to the latest value. Retaining 8 to 16 observations per variable, TRESS records the lowest mean test MSE and MAE among the methods compared on all four benchmarks. Serving 32 successive query times from one encoded history reduces CPU inference time by a factor of 2.12--2.60 across the four datasets. The code is at https://github.com/SSMa913/NICLab-TRESS.

abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) can improve robot learning by jointly predicting future visual states and actions, but generating a visual future at every replanning step is expensive and sometimes unnecessary. This raises a critical question: when should a robot policy imagine the future? In this paper, we propose Bind-WAM, a binding-uncertainty-guided WAM for selective future imagination. Bind-WAM introduces language-object binding uncertainty, selectively invoking joint future-action generation when the current observation does not support stable task-relevant action generation. An offline labeling pipeline uses complete demonstrations and action context to identify task-relevant objects and detect reference mismatch, invisibility, and identity drift. The resulting pseudo-labels supervise a lightweight router that predicts binding uncertainty from the current observation and language instruction. At inference, a shared WAM policy invokes selective future imagination according to the predicted uncertainty and its change between consecutive replanning steps. Simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate that Bind-WAM can establish binding uncertainty as a strong, interpretable signal for selective future imagination.

abstract: Recent advances in generative modeling have reshaped recommender systems by formulating recommendation as a next-item generation problem. Existing retrieval approaches primarily follow two paradigms: user-to-item (U2I) methods represent user context using one or a few deterministic embeddings, which limits the ability to capture diverse and multi-mode interests, while semantic-ID-based autoregressive (SID-AR) methods model more expressive distributions but suffer from quantization errors and the low throughput of sequential decoding. To address these limitations, we propose X-Rec to directly learn the recommendation distribution in the continuous item embedding space through flow matching and generate embedding triggers for approximate nearest neighbor retrieval. X-Rec incorporates three key designs to make this formulation effective and efficient. First, we introduce anchor conditioning to decompose generation into coarse semantic-region selection and fine-grained refinement. Second, we adopt Riemannian flow matching to align generative trajectories with the hyperspherical geometry of item embeddings. Third, we design a late-interaction diffusion Transformer that restricts repeated velocity-field estimation to the final Transformer layer. On a streaming benchmark, X-Rec substantially outperforms U2I baselines, matches the retrieval quality of SID-AR methods, and delivers 3.46x higher inference throughput than SID-AR. X-Rec has also been deployed as a new retrieval source for a specific vertical content on TikTok, where two consecutive launches have yielded significant improvements in both vertical engagement (+4.1484%) and general engagement (+0.0111%).

abstract: Hyper-Connections (HC) expand the residual stream of a Transformer into $N$ parallel streams, and manifold-constrained HC (mHC) stabilizes them at scale. However, mHC benefits little from more than four streams, partly because each sublayer writes a single output to all streams, limiting how differently they can be updated. In this work, we propose TPHC, which integrates tensor-parallel (TP) shards with HC streams to promote greater independence across streams. Specifically, we route a separate mixture of the residual streams to each TP shard and keep the individual shard outputs separate during write-back, so each stream can receive a different mixture of those outputs. This design makes the residual-stream updates more expressive without adding parameters or FLOPs to the attention or FFN sublayers. With native support for stream sharding under TP, TPHC requires only 9% more training time than mHC on an 8B model when both use four streams. Increasing the number of streams from four to sixteen raises its training time by only 19%. On a 1.1B model trained on 100B tokens, TPHC reduces validation loss by 0.7-1.0% and raises average zero-shot accuracy across six commonsense reasoning benchmarks by 0.3-0.7 percentage points relative to mHC at matched stream counts $N\in\{4,8,16\}$. Our code is available at https://github.com/wuyou2002/TPHC.

abstract: We study Gaussian kernel approximation and regularized logistic classification on a connected compact smooth embedded manifold $X\subset\mathbb R^d$ without boundary and of intrinsic dimension $\varrho$. Two main challenges are to derive a fast oracle inequality without assuming a bounded Bayes function and to construct Gaussian approximants that exploit both the intrinsic dimension and the target's regularity without saturation. We address the first challenge through a Bernstein-type inequality whose constant depends linearly on the supremum norm of the predictor. Combined with localized complexity estimates, this yields an oracle inequality over separable normed function spaces. To address the second challenge, we establish a uniform Sobolev operator expansion and cancel its lower-order bias terms using a signed combination of Gaussian kernel integral operators at different bandwidths. Real interpolation then gives an $L_2(X)$ approximation error of order $γ^α$ for functions in $B^α_{2,\infty}(X)$, where $γ$ is the bandwidth. By constructing the approximants directly on the manifold without ambient extension, we obtain a squared Gaussian RKHS norm bound of order $γ^{-\varrho}$. This construction thus overcomes second-order saturation while retaining norm control governed by the intrinsic dimension. When the marginal distribution has a density $g\in L_p(X)$, these results yield the logistic excess-risk rate $\bigl((\log n)^{\varrho+1}/n\bigr)^{4α(1-1/p)/(4α(1-1/p)+3\varrho)}$. We further show that clipping predictions yields the faster clipped logistic excess-risk rate $\bigl((\log n)^{\varrho+2}/n\bigr)^{2α(1-1/p)/(2α(1-1/p)+\varrho)}$. For bounded densities, its polynomial exponent matches that of the minimax optimal rate for squared-loss regression, and its corresponding excess misclassification risk also matches the minimax optimal rate.

abstract: We introduce a class of demand models for market-level data. The models can be estimated by linear instrumental variables regression while accommodating substitution patterns far richer than the logit and nested logit models they embed. They are built from closed-form inverse market share functions through a generator analogous to McFadden's generalized extreme value generating function, but acting on market shares. Constructive results allow arbitrary nesting structures, including overlapping nests and partial membership, yielding inverse-share analogs of generalized extreme value models. The class is consistent with utility maximization and strictly larger than the class of regular additive random utility models.

abstract: Platforms summarize providers' past achievements into credentials that buyers use to judge quality. Generative AI can now produce much of the work those achievements certify, raising fears that those quality signals are worthless. We audit how well such credentials stay informative in Kaggle's 2010-2026 archive, where medals are won on predictions scored against withheld answers and two evaluation formats ran side by side. Across 444,698 participations, a medal's power to predict performance sits almost entirely in its first year, in both formats and eras. Fresh medals kept most of their value through the AI transition. About half of the collapse in the informativeness of one format's medals is institutional: the platform had been phasing out that format before AI, and its medal stock aged out on schedule. Old medals look more informative only in isolation. The platform's official lifetime-tier display discards up to a sixth of the medals' predictive power. A recency-weighted index fit before the AI era explains AI-era performance about 13% better than the tiers and selects entrants who perform better on average, though the tiers still identify extreme top performers better. Displaying a recent-performance summary alongside the lifetime tiers would recover the discarded information for buyers.

abstract: Recommendation and Ranking (R&R) models, particularly in digital advertising, require massive inference throughput but exhibit extreme sensitivity to precision loss. Unlike Large Language Models (LLMs) that frequently tolerate quantization-induced accuracy drops of 1% or more, production-grade R&R models enforce a stringent launch bar: model quality must remain within a 0.01% Normalized Entropy (NE) margin relative to the baseline, which commonly uses FP16 or FP32. This tight constraint has historically hindered the adoption of aggressive quantization in this domain. In this paper, we present an empirical evaluation of both MXFP8 and the 6-bit MXFP6 format for industrial-scale R&R inference on the AMD MI350X architecture. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first paper, across R&R and LLM domains, that reports significant speedups from native MXFP6 GEMMs, which quantize both weights and activations and compute directly on 6-bit elements, without sacrificing model quality. We demonstrate that we can selectively apply this 6-bit format to maximize overall QPS gain without breaching the strict NE parity threshold. We further show that MXFP8 is a viable alternative to row-wise FP8: the two formats have nearly the same accuracy on our models, so the faster kernel can be chosen for each GEMM shape. On two production ads ranking models, our implementation shows measured GEMM kernel speedups over FP16 of 1.33--1.55x for MXFP8 and 1.73--1.99x for MXFP6 across all supported linear layers, and up to 2.90x for MXFP6 on individual layers, alongside end-to-end (E2E) inference throughput gains from selective MXFP6 of 1.5--5.3% for Model A and 7.6--14.3% for Model B over their FP8 configurations.

abstract: Advancing from individual embodied intelligence to swarm embodied intelligence is a key step toward scalable, general-purpose embodied intelligence. Complex tasks often require multiple agents to divide responsibilities, coordinate handovers, and manipulate shared objects collaboratively. However, existing robot learning methods rely primarily on individual demonstrations, which provide limited supervision for modeling dependencies among agent actions, while collecting multi-robot demonstrations at scale remains difficult. Human egocentric demonstrations offer a scalable alternative, yet distributed observations from multiple participants cannot directly supervise decentralized policies. We introduce EgoSwarm, the first robot learning framework for learning decentralized multi-robot collaboration from human swarm demonstrations. EgoSwarm collects more than 50 hours of collaborative experience using a robot-free multi-person egocentric system. We introduce the Swarm Interaction Packet (SIP) and Swarm Interaction Token (SIT) to recover cross-agent interaction relations from distributed observations and transform this experience into local supervision consistent with deployment-time information constraints. We further propose SwarmVLA, which transfers knowledge of swarm behavior to decentralized policies conditioned on local observations, local history, and limited neighbor messages. SwarmVLA achieves a mean success rate of 72.2% across three categories of multi-robot collaborative tasks. Project page:https://xitong-c.github.io/EgoSwarm_Page/.

abstract: In many power systems, installed wind and solar now exceed peak electricity demand. In very sunny or windy periods, curtailing renewable generation becomes a precondition for grid stability. While turning off wind turbines and solar panels is technically easy, support schemes often give renewables an economic incentive to keep producing at negative prices. This paper studies wind and solar energy in Germany, estimating, for each cohort of generators, hour by hour the incentives implied by two decades of support policy. It then sets those incentives against observed behavior, using a new estimate of market-based curtailment built from reanalysis weather data. I find that in 2025, at prices below -50 EUR/MWh, almost all wind generators had an incentive to stop producing, but only half of them did. Nearly two thirds of solar capacity had no incentive to curtail at all, mostly because it receives a feed-in tariff that shields it from wholesale prices. Of the exposed remainder, about one in seven cut production. Low exposure and response rates inflate subsidy payments and make the power system harder to operate safely. I conclude that a further expansion of wind and solar requires them to respond to price signals, which depends on policy makers providing proper incentives and on generators acting on them.

abstract: Equality before the law is a human right, and access to high-quality legal aid for indigent defendants is essential to enforce it. In a context where all defendants have access to a lawyer, I study the impact of denying legal aid on court outcomes. I combine double machine learning and a new administrative dataset linking aid to court outcomes in New South Wales, Australia, to learn the assignment function, whose inputs are known. I find that applicants who fail the means test and hire private lawyers are 10 percentage points less likely to be incarcerated than if they passed and relied on legal aid. Given an average incarceration length of nearly four years, this gap is significant. However, I find evidence suggesting that they spend more time in jail if they are incarcerated. A government preference for broad access to aid over allocated time per case could explain this pattern. Keywords: Indigent Defense, Crime, Criminal Justice. JEL: I30, K14, H44.

abstract: Ensuring robust safety alignment of large language models (LLMs) is increasingly difficult as adversarial attacks evolve and outpace alignment pipelines built on pre-collected data. Existing co-evolutionary frameworks let the defender chase a moving attacker, yet their training dynamics expose two compounding pathologies: \emph{attack strategy collapse}, where the attacker overfits to a narrow set of high-reward rewrites, and \emph{defense adversarial forgetting}, where the defender loses competence against earlier attacks as the attack distribution drifts. Existing remedies are partial: attacker-side diversity rewards score textual novelty rather than strategy novelty, and defender-side replay relies on discrete judge scores that ignore estimation uncertainty, response stochasticity, and defender non-stationarity. We introduce \textbf{\method}, a diversity-driven adversarial co-evolution framework that targets both pathologies jointly. On the attacker side, \method couples an explicit two-dimensional strategy space (risk category $\times$ attack style) with a \emph{normalized marginal coverage gain} reward, providing a bounded, non-vanishing exploration signal at the strategy layer. On the defender side, \method maintains a unified \emph{Bayesian adversarial replay pool} whose Beta--Bernoulli threat posteriors are refreshed by time decay and sampled via Thompson sampling, anchoring defender training to an evolving threat landscape. Across standard safety, automated-attacker, and general-capability benchmarks, \method improves robustness to out-of-distribution attacks while preserving general capabilities, and yields broader attacker strategy coverage.
